title: 3Sum
statement:
Given a list of integers `nums`, return every set of three values that adds up to 0. The three values must come from three different positions in the list, and each distinct triplet should be reported only once, even if it can be formed in several ways (for example [-1, 0, 1] and [0, 1, -1] count as the same triplet).

The triplets may be returned in any order, and the numbers inside a triplet may be in any order. If no triplet adds up to 0, return an empty list.

Constraints: 3 <= len(nums) <= 3000; -10^5 <= nums[i] <= 10^5.

examples.explanation: Two distinct triplets work: -3 + 1 + 2 and -1 + 0 + 1. The repeated -3s and 1s do not create extra copies.
All four zeros are interchangeable, so the single triplet [0, 0, 0] is reported once.
Only the values -2, 0 and 2 can be combined, and the repeated 0 and 2 still give just one triplet.

title: Design Add and Search Words Data Structure
statement:
Design a structure that stores words and answers lookups in which some letters are unknown.

Implement the `WordDictionary` class:
- `WordDictionary()` creates an empty dictionary.
- `addWord(word)` stores `word`.
- `search(word)` returns `True` if some stored word matches `word`, and `False` otherwise. `word` may contain dots, and each `.` matches exactly one letter of any kind. A match must have the same length.

Each test creates a dictionary and calls its methods in order. The expected output lists what each call returns, with `null` for the constructor and for `addWord`.

Constraints: 1 <= len(word) <= 25; added words use lowercase English letters; search patterns use lowercase letters and `.`; at most 10^4 calls in total.

examples.explanation: "c.t" matches both stored words; "ca" is only a prefix; ".." would need a two-letter word.
Dots can stand for any letters, but "m...n" has five characters and "moon" has four.
Nothing matches before any word is added.

title: Alien Dictionary
statement:
An alien language uses lowercase English letters, but in an unknown order. You're given a list of words from its dictionary, sorted by the alien alphabet the way a normal dictionary sorts words: compare letter by letter, the first differing letter decides, and a word comes before any longer word it is a prefix of.

Return a string with every letter that appears in the words, each exactly once, in an order consistent with the list. If several orders work, return any of them. If no order can make the list sorted, return `""`.

Constraints: 1 <= len(words) <= 1000; 1 <= len(word) <= 20; words use lowercase English letters.

examples.explanation: Neighboring words give p before b, k before p and b before q, so the only order is k, p, b, q.
"app" is a prefix of "apple", so it would have to come first; no alphabet can fix that.
Only n before o is known. Any order with n ahead of o, such as "mno" or "nom", is accepted.

title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock
statement:
You're given a list `prices` where `prices[i]` is the price of one share of a stock on day `i`. You may make a single trade: buy on one day, then sell on a later day. Return the largest profit that trade can earn.

If every possible trade would lose money (or there is only one day), the best move is not to trade at all, so return 0.

Constraints: 1 <= len(prices) <= 10^5; 0 <= prices[i] <= 10^4.

examples.explanation: Buy at 2 (day 3) and sell at 8 (day 4): 8 - 2 = 6.
Prices only fall, so any trade loses money and the answer is 0.
The lowest price (1) comes after the highest (8), so the best trade is 6 -> 8 for a profit of 2, not 8 - 1.

title: Binary Tree Level Order Traversal
statement:
You're given the root of a binary tree. Return its values level by level: a list whose first entry holds the root's value, the next holds the values one level down, and so on. Within a level, list the values from left to right.

An empty tree gives an empty list. Each node is a `TreeNode` with `val`, `left` and `right`; the class is already defined for you. In the examples, a tree is written in level order with `null` for a missing child.

Constraints: 0 to 2000 nodes; -1000 <= val <= 1000.

examples.explanation: 4 is the left child of 2 and 5 the right child of 3; they share the third level.
A single node makes a single level.
No nodes, no levels.

title: Binary Tree Maximum Path Sum
statement:
You're given the root of a non-empty binary tree whose values can be negative. A path is a chain of nodes where each consecutive pair is joined by an edge (parent to child or child to parent) and no node appears twice. A path has at least one node and doesn't have to pass through the root.

Return the largest sum of node values over all paths in the tree. Each node is a `TreeNode` with `val`, `left` and `right`; the class is already defined for you. In the examples, a tree is written in level order with `null` for a missing child.

Constraints: 1 to 3 * 10^4 nodes; -1000 <= val <= 1000.

examples.explanation: The best path is 2 -> 3. Adding -1 would only lower the sum.
The path 8 -> 6 sums to 14 and never touches the negative root; going through the root (4, -5, 8, 6) gives only 13.
A path needs at least one node, so the only choice is the root itself.

title: Climbing Stairs
statement:
A staircase has `n` steps and you start at the bottom. On every move you climb either 1 step or 2 steps. Count the different sequences of moves that take you exactly to step `n`.

Two sequences are different if their moves differ anywhere, so climbing 1 then 2 and climbing 2 then 1 count as two separate ways.

Constraints: 1 <= n <= 45 (the answer fits in a 32-bit signed integer).

examples.explanation: Either two single steps (1+1) or one double step (2).
Eight different orderings of 1s and 2s add up to 5.

title: Clone Graph
statement:
You're given one node of a connected, undirected graph. Each node is a `Node` with an integer `val` and a list `neighbors` of the nodes it's connected to; the class is already defined for you. Return a deep copy of the graph: brand-new `Node` objects with the same values and the same connections, starting from the copy of the node you were given.

The copy must not share any node with the original, so returning the input (or linking copies to original nodes) fails. In the examples, a graph is written as an adjacency list: entry i lists the neighbors of the node whose `val` is i + 1, and you're given the node with `val` 1. An empty graph is `[]`, and you receive `None`.

Constraints: 0 to 100 nodes; node values are 1 to n and distinct; no repeated edges and no self-loops; the graph is connected.

examples.explanation: A triangle: every node links to the other two, and the copy must too.
One node with no neighbors.
No graph at all, so the function gets None and returns None.

title: Coin Change
statement:
You're given a list of distinct coin values `coins` and a target `amount`. You have an unlimited supply of every coin. Return the fewest coins that add up to exactly `amount`, or -1 if no combination of coins can make it.

Making an amount of 0 takes 0 coins. Be careful: always taking the biggest coin that fits does not always give the fewest coins.

Constraints: 1 <= len(coins) <= 12; 1 <= coins[i] <= 1000, all distinct; 0 <= amount <= 300.

Every combination of 4s and 6s is even, so 7 can't be made.

title: Combination Sum
statement:
You're given a list of distinct positive integers `candidates` and a positive integer `target`. Find every unique combination of candidates that adds up to `target`. Each candidate may be used any number of times, and two combinations are different only if some number is used a different number of times.

Return the combinations as a list of lists, in any order. The order of numbers inside a combination doesn't matter either, so [2, 3] and [3, 2] are the same combination and must appear only once. Return an empty list if none exist.

Constraints: 1 <= len(candidates) <= 12; 1 <= candidates[i] <= 40, all distinct; 1 <= target <= 40.

Every candidate is bigger than the target, so nothing works.

title: Construct Binary Tree from Preorder and Inorder Traversal
statement:
You're given two lists that describe the same binary tree: `preorder` lists its values in preorder (node, then left subtree, then right subtree) and `inorder` lists them in inorder (left subtree, then node, then right subtree). All values are distinct.

Rebuild the tree and return its root. Each node is a `TreeNode` with `val`, `left` and `right`; the class is already defined for you. In the examples, the returned tree is written in level order with `null` for a missing child.

Constraints: 1 <= len(preorder) == len(inorder) <= 3000; -3000 <= val <= 3000; both lists come from one valid tree.

Each value sits left of its parent in inorder, so the tree is a chain going left.

title: Container With Most Water
statement:
You're given a list `height` where `height[i]` is the height of a vertical wall standing at position `i` on a number line. Choose any two walls; together with the ground they form a container, and the water it holds is the distance between the two walls times the height of the shorter one. Walls can't be tilted, and the walls in between are ignored.

Return the largest amount of water any pair of walls can hold.

Constraints: 2 <= len(height) <= 10^5; 0 <= height[i] <= 10^4.

examples.explanation: The walls of height 9 (position 1) and 8 (position 5) are 4 apart and the shorter is 8: 4 * 8 = 32.
Two walls of height 5 that are 1 apart hold 1 * 5 = 5.
The two walls of height 6 are 5 apart: 5 * 6 = 30. The short walls between them do not matter.

title: Contains Duplicate
statement:
You're given a list of integers `nums`. Return `True` if some value shows up at least twice, and `False` if every value in the list is different.

Constraints: 1 <= len(nums) <= 10^5; -10^9 <= nums[i] <= 10^9.

examples.explanation: The value 7 appears at positions 1 and 3.
All four values are different.
A single element cannot repeat.

title: Counting Bits
statement:
Given a non-negative integer `n`, return a list `ans` of length n + 1 where ans[i] is the number of 1 bits in the binary form of i, for every i from 0 to n.

Counting the bits of each number separately works, but try to do it in a single pass by reusing answers you have already computed.

Constraints: 0 <= n <= 10^5.

examples.explanation: 0 is 0, 1 is 1 and 2 is 10 in binary, so the counts are 0, 1, 1.
3 is 11 (two 1s), 4 is 100 (one) and 5 is 101 (two).
Only the number 0 itself, which has no 1 bits.

title: Course Schedule
statement:
There are `num_courses` courses numbered 0 to num_courses - 1. Each pair [a, b] in `prerequisites` means you must finish course b before you can start course a. Return `True` if it is possible to finish every course, and `False` otherwise, for example when courses wait on each other in a loop.

Some courses may have no prerequisites at all, and the same pair can appear more than once.

Constraints: 1 <= num_courses <= 2000; 0 <= len(prerequisites) <= 5000; a != b in every pair; 0 <= a, b < num_courses.
signature: def can_finish(num_courses: int, prerequisites: list[list[int]]) -> bool:

Each course needs the other first, so neither can ever start.
Course 3 needs both 1 and 2, which both need 0. Two paths meeting again is not a cycle.

title: Decode Ways
statement:
A message made of capital letters was turned into digits using A = 1, B = 2, ..., Z = 26. Given the digit string `s`, return how many different letter messages it could have come from.

A split is valid when the string is cut into pieces of one or two digits, every piece is a number from 1 to 26, and no piece starts with 0. So "6" and "10" are fine but "06" and "0" are not. If no valid split exists, return 0.

Constraints: 1 <= len(s) <= 100; s contains only digits; the answer fits in a 32-bit signed integer.

examples.explanation: Read it as 1-2-3, 12-3 or 1-23, which spell "ABC", "LC" and "AW".
2-6-10 and 26-10 are valid. 2-61 and any split that ends in a lone 0 are not.
"50" is too big and "06" starts with a zero, so the 0 can never be placed.

title: Encode and Decode Strings
statement:
You need to send a list of strings over a channel that only carries a single string. Implement the `Codec` class:
- `encode(strs)` turns a list of strings into one string.
- `decode(s)` takes a string produced by `encode` and returns the original list of strings exactly.

The strings can contain any characters at all: digits, commas, `#`, newlines, non-English letters, or nothing (an empty string), so you can't pick a separator and assume it never appears in the data. An empty list and a list holding one empty string are different inputs and must come back differently. Each test encodes with one `Codec` object and decodes with a separate one, so the encoded string has to carry everything on its own.

Constraints: 0 to 200 strings; each string has 0 to 3,000 characters, and may contain any Unicode characters.

examples.explanation: decode(encode(strs)) must return the same list.
An empty list must survive the round trip as an empty list.
Empty strings and a # inside a string must come back unchanged.

title: Find Median from Data Stream
statement:
The median of a group of numbers is the middle value once they are sorted; if the group has an even count, it is the average of the two middle values. Numbers arrive one at a time, and you must be able to report the median of everything seen so far at any moment.

Implement the `MedianFinder` class:
- `MedianFinder()` creates an empty finder.
- `addNum(num)` adds the integer `num` to the stream.
- `findMedian()` returns the median of all numbers added so far, as a float.

`findMedian` is only called after at least one `addNum`. Each test creates a finder and makes its calls in order. The expected output lists what each call returns, with `null` for the constructor and for `addNum`. Results are compared with a small tolerance, so 2 and 2.0 are both fine.

Constraints: -100,000 <= num <= 100,000; at most 50,000 calls in total.

examples.explanation: After 5 and 15 the median is (5 + 15) / 2 = 10.0; after 1 it is the middle of [1, 5, 15], 5.0; after 20 it is (5 + 15) / 2 = 10.0 again.
A single number is its own median.
[3, 3, 9] has median 3.0; adding another 9 makes the middle pair 3 and 9, so the median is 6.0.

title: Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array
statement:
A list of distinct integers `nums` was sorted in ascending order and then rotated: some number of elements were moved from the front to the back, keeping their order. Rotating by zero is allowed, so the list may still be fully sorted.

Return the smallest value in `nums`. Your solution should run in O(log n) time, which rules out scanning the whole list.

Constraints: 1 <= len(nums) <= 5000; all values are distinct; -5000 <= nums[i] <= 5000.

examples.explanation: The list was rotated so that 2 follows 9; the smallest value is 2.
A rotation of zero leaves the list sorted, so the minimum is the first element.
A single element is its own minimum.

title: Graph Valid Tree
statement:
You're given `n` nodes labeled 0 to n - 1 and a list of undirected edges, where `[a, b]` connects nodes `a` and `b`. Return `True` if these edges form a single tree, and `False` otherwise.

A tree is connected (every node can reach every other node) and has no cycles. No edge is listed twice, and no edge connects a node to itself.

title: Group Anagrams
statement:
Given a list of strings `strs`, group together the strings that are anagrams of each other (they use the same letters the same number of times). Return the groups as a list of lists; every input string must appear in exactly one group, including repeated strings and empty strings.

The groups can be returned in any order, and the strings inside a group can be in any order.

Constraints: 1 <= len(strs) <= 10^4; 0 <= len(strs[i]) <= 100; every string contains only lowercase English letters.

examples.explanation: "stop", "pots" and "tops" share letters, as do "cat" and "act"; "dog" stands alone.
A single empty string forms one group by itself.

title: House Robber
statement:
You're given a list `nums` where nums[i] is the amount of money inside the i-th house along a street. You may rob any set of houses, but you must not rob two houses that are next to each other. Return the largest total you can rob.

An empty street gives 0.

Constraints: 0 <= len(nums) <= 400; 0 <= nums[i] <= 400.

examples.explanation: Rob the houses holding 9 and 8. Houses 1 and 3 aren't neighbours.
Rob the first, fourth and last houses: 4 + 9 + 4. Taking every other house reaches at most 11.
A single house is simply robbed.

title: House Robber II
statement:
This time the houses stand in a circle: the first house is a neighbour of the last one as well as the second. You still must not rob two neighbouring houses. Given `nums` with the money in each house in order around the circle, return the largest total you can rob.

With a single house there is nobody next to it, so you can rob it.

Constraints: 1 <= len(nums) <= 400; 0 <= nums[i] <= 400.

examples.explanation: The first and last houses are neighbours, so you can't take both 4s. Take 4 + 2 instead.
With three houses in a circle every pair is adjacent, so you can only rob one.
A lone house has no neighbours.

title: Implement Trie (Prefix Tree)
statement:
A trie, or prefix tree, stores a set of words so that lookups by whole word or by prefix are fast. It is the structure behind autocomplete and spell checkers.

Implement the `Trie` class:
- `Trie()` creates an empty trie.
- `insert(word)` adds `word` to the trie.
- `search(word)` returns `True` if `word` was inserted earlier, and `False` otherwise.
- `startsWith(prefix)` returns `True` if at least one inserted word begins with `prefix`, and `False` otherwise.

Each test creates a trie and calls its methods in order. The expected output lists what each call returns, with `null` for the constructor and for `insert`.

Constraints: 1 <= len(word), len(prefix) <= 2000; words and prefixes use lowercase English letters only; at most 3 * 10^4 calls in total.

Add the new interval to the list and merge it with every interval it overlaps, so that the result is still sorted by start and still has no overlaps. Return the resulting list.

Two intervals that share only an endpoint, such as `[1, 4]` and `[4, 6]`, count as overlapping and become one interval. `intervals` may be empty.

title: Invert Binary Tree
statement:
You're given the root of a binary tree. Mirror it: at every node, swap the left and right children. Return the root of the mirrored tree.

You may change the tree in place or build a new one. The tree may be empty (`None`). Each node is a `TreeNode` with `val`, `left` and `right`; the class is already defined for you. In the examples, a tree is written in level order with `null` for a missing child.

Constraints: 0 to 2000 nodes; -100 <= val <= 100.

The only child moves from the left side to the right side.
An empty tree stays empty.

title: Jump Game
statement:
You're given a list `nums` where nums[i] is the farthest you can jump forward from index i (you may also jump any shorter distance, including 1). You start at index 0. Return `True` if you can reach the last index, and `False` otherwise.

A 0 means you can't move forward from that spot, so landing on one is a dead end unless you got past it earlier.

Constraints: 1 <= len(nums) <= 400; 0 <= nums[i] <= 10^5.

In a binary search tree, every value in a node's left subtree is smaller than the node and every value in its right subtree is larger. All values are distinct. title: Linked List Cycle
statement:
You're given the head of a singly linked list. Return `True` if following `next` pointers from the head ever revisits a node, meaning the list loops back on itself, and `False` if the walk reaches the end (`None`).

Each node is a `ListNode` with `val` and `next`; the class is already defined for you. Constraints: 0 to 10^4 nodes; -10^5 <= val <= 10^5.

A single node whose next pointer is itself.

title: Longest Common Subsequence
statement:
Given two strings `text1` and `text2`, return the length of their longest common subsequence: the longest sequence of characters that appears in both strings in the same relative order, though not necessarily next to each other.

If the strings share no characters the answer is 0, and either string may be empty.

title: Longest Consecutive Sequence
statement:
You're given an unsorted list of integers, `nums`. Return the length of the longest run of consecutive integers (each one exactly 1 more than the one before) whose members all appear in `nums`. The numbers do not have to be next to each other in the list, or in order.

A value that appears several times counts once. For an empty list the answer is 0. Aim for O(n) time, which rules out sorting.

Constraints: 0 <= len(nums) <= 100,000; -10^9 <= nums[i] <= 10^9.

examples.explanation: 29, 30, 31 is a run of 3, and 5, 6, 7, 8 is a run of 4, so the answer is 4.
An empty list has no run at all.

title: Longest Increasing Subsequence
statement:
Given a list of integers `nums`, return the length of its longest strictly increasing subsequence. A subsequence keeps the original order of the elements but may skip some of them, and strictly increasing means every chosen value is bigger than the one before it.

You only need the length, not the subsequence itself. An empty list gives 0.

Constraints: 0 <= len(nums) <= 400; -10^4 <= nums[i] <= 10^4.

3, 5, 8, 9 (or 3, 4, 8, 9) skips the elements in between.

title: Longest Palindromic Substring
statement:
Given a string `s`, return its longest palindromic substring: a run of consecutive characters that reads the same forwards and backwards. A single character is a palindrome, so the answer is never empty.

Several palindromes could tie for longest on some strings, but the tests only use inputs where the longest one is unique, so you won't have to break ties.

Constraints: 1 <= len(s) <= 1000; `s` contains digits and English letters.

Return the length of the longest substring that could consist of one repeated letter after those changes. You only need to report the length, not make the changes.

title: Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters
statement:
Given a string `s`, find the longest substring (a run of consecutive characters) in which no character appears twice, and return its length. The string may be empty, in which case the answer is 0.

Constraints: 0 <= len(s) <= 5 * 10^4; `s` contains printable ASCII characters (letters, digits, symbols and spaces).

title: Lowest Common Ancestor of a Binary Search Tree
statement:
You're given the root of a binary search tree and two different nodes of it, `p` and `q`. Return their lowest common ancestor: the deepest node that has both `p` and `q` in its subtree. A node counts as part of its own subtree, so if `p` sits above `q`, the answer is `p`.

In the examples, the tree is written in level order with `null` for a missing child, and nodes are named by their values.

title: Maximum Depth of Binary Tree
statement:
You're given the root of a binary tree. Return its maximum depth: the number of nodes on the longest path that starts at the root and ends at a leaf.

An empty tree (`root` is `None`) has depth 0. Each node is a `TreeNode` with `val`, `left` and `right`; the class is already defined for you. In the examples, a tree is written in level order with `null` for a missing child.

title: Maximum Product Subarray
statement:
Given a list of integers `nums`, find the contiguous, non-empty run of elements whose product is as large as possible, and return that product.

The list may contain negative numbers and zeros, so the best run is not always the whole list. A run of one element counts.

Constraints: 1 <= len(nums) <= 2 * 10^4; -10 <= nums[i] <= 10; the answer fits in a 32-bit signed integer.

title: Maximum Subarray
statement:
Given a list of integers `nums`, find the contiguous, non-empty run of elements with the largest sum and return that sum.

The list can contain negative numbers, and it can be made up of negative numbers only; in that case the answer is the single largest (least negative) element.

Constraints: 1 <= len(nums) <= 10^5; -10^4 <= nums[i] <= 10^4.

title: Meeting Rooms
statement:
You're given a list of `intervals`, where `intervals[i] = [start, end]` is one meeting that begins at `start` and ends at `end`. Return `True` if a single person could attend every meeting, and `False` if any two meetings overlap.

Constraints: 0 to 5,000 meetings; 0 <= start < end <= 1,000,000.

title: Meeting Rooms II
statement:
You're given a list of `intervals`, where `intervals[i] = [start, end]` is one meeting. Return the minimum number of rooms needed so that every meeting gets a room and no two meetings are in the same room at the same time.

A room becomes free the moment its meeting ends, so a meeting that ends at time `t` and another that starts at `t` can use the same room. The meetings may be given in any order, and the list may be empty (zero rooms).

Constraints: 0 to 5,000 meetings; 0 <= start < end <= 1,000,000.

title: Merge Intervals
statement:
You're given a list of `intervals`, each written as `[start, end]`, in no particular order. Merge every group of overlapping intervals into one interval that spans the whole group, and return the merged intervals sorted by start.

Intervals that share only an endpoint, such as `[1, 4]` and `[4, 5]`, count as overlapping. An interval can also sit entirely inside another. If the input is empty, return an empty list.

Constraints: 0 to 5,000 intervals; 0 <= start <= end <= 10,000.

[2, 3] and [4, 5] sit inside [1, 10], so the merged interval keeps the end 10.

title: Merge K Sorted Lists
statement:
You're given `lists`, an array holding the heads of k singly linked lists. Each list is already sorted from smallest to largest (equal values may repeat). Merge all of them into a single sorted linked list by relinking the nodes you were given, and return the head of the merged list.

title: Minimum Window Substring
statement:
You're given two strings, `s` and `t`. Find the shortest substring of `s` that contains every character of `t`, counting repeats: if `t` has two copies of a letter, the substring needs at least two copies of it too (extra characters are allowed). Return that substring, or an empty string if no substring of `s` qualifies.

The tests only use inputs where the shortest window is unique, so you won't have to choose between ties. Matching is case sensitive.

title: Missing Number
statement:
You're given a list `nums` holding n distinct integers, each between 0 and n inclusive. That range contains n + 1 values, so exactly one of them is absent. Return the missing value.

The numbers come in no particular order. An empty list means n = 0, so the missing number is 0.

title: Non-overlapping Intervals
statement:
You're given a list of `intervals`, each written as `[start, end]`. Return the fewest intervals you have to remove so that none of the remaining intervals overlap.

Two intervals overlap when they share some stretch of the number line. Intervals that only touch at an endpoint, like `[1, 2]` and `[2, 3]`, do not overlap. Only the number of removals is asked for, not which intervals to remove.

statement:

Water on a cell flows to any neighbour (up, down, left or right) whose height is less than or equal to its own, and water on a border cell drains straight into the ocean that border touches.

title: Palindromic Substrings
statement:
Given a string `s`, count how many of its substrings are palindromes (they read the same forwards and backwards). Substrings are counted by position, so two equal substrings taken from different places each count, and every single character counts as a palindrome of length one.

statement:
Given a list of integers `nums`, return a new list `answer` of the same length where `answer[i]` is the product of every element of `nums` except `nums[i]`.

title: Valid Parentheses
statement:
You're given a string `s` made up only of the bracket characters `(`, `)`, `[`, `]`, `{` and `}`. Decide whether the brackets are balanced.

A string is balanced when every opening bracket is closed by a bracket of the same kind, brackets close in the reverse order they were opened, and no closing bracket shows up without an opener waiting for it. An empty string is balanced.

Return `True` if `s` is balanced and `False` otherwise.

Constraints: 0 <= len(s) <= 10^4.

examples.explanation: Each opener is closed by its own kind, innermost first.
The square bracket opens inside the round one, but the round one closes first.
Two brackets are opened and never closed.

title: Validate Binary Search Tree
statement:
You're given the root of a binary tree. Return `True` if it is a valid binary search tree, and `False` otherwise.

In a valid binary search tree, every value in a node's left subtree is strictly smaller than the node's value, every value in its right subtree is strictly larger, and both subtrees are valid binary search trees themselves. Equal values are not allowed. Each node is a `TreeNode` with `val`, `left` and `right`; the class is already defined for you. In the examples, a tree is written in level order with `null` for a missing child.

Constraints: 1 to 10^4 nodes; -2^31 <= val <= 2^31 - 1.

examples.explanation: Everything left of 5 is smaller and everything right of it is larger, and the same holds under 3.
6 is a fine right child for 3, but it sits in 5's left subtree and is larger than 5.
Equal values aren't allowed, so a left child equal to its parent breaks the rule.

title: Word Break
statement:
Given a string `s` and a list of words `word_dict`, decide whether `s` can be cut into a sequence of dictionary words placed end to end with nothing left over. The same word may be used as many times as you like.

Return `True` if such a split exists and `False` otherwise. The dictionary words are distinct and `s` is never empty.

Constraints: 1 <= len(s) <= 300; 1 <= len(word_dict) <= 1000; every word has 1 to 20 characters; all strings are lowercase English letters.
signature: def word_break(s: str, word_dict: list[str]) -> bool:

examples.explanation: "book" followed by "shelf".
"sun" + "day" + "morn" leaves "ing" over, and nothing else fits.
"goal" + "special" works. Taking the longer "goals" first leaves "pecial", which is a dead end.

title: Word Search
statement:
You're given a grid of lowercase letters, `board`, and a string `word`. Return `True` if `word` can be spelled by starting at some cell and repeatedly stepping to a cell directly above, below, left or right of the current one, and `False` otherwise.

Each step must land on the next letter of the word, and a path may not use the same cell more than once. Diagonal steps are not allowed.

Constraints: 1 <= rows, columns <= 6; 1 <= len(word) <= 15; the board and the word contain lowercase English letters only.
signature: def exist(board: List[List[str]], word: str) -> bool:

examples.explanation: r, a, n, i is a path: right along the top, then down the last column.
p and o are adjacent, but s is not adjacent to o, so the path breaks.
There is only one a, and a path cannot use a cell twice.

title: Word Search II
statement:
You're given a grid of lowercase letters, `board`, and a list of distinct words. Return every word from the list that can be spelled on the board.

A word is spelled by starting on any cell and moving to a horizontally or vertically adjacent cell for each next letter. Within one word, a cell can be used at most once. List each found word once, in any order.

Constraints: 1 <= rows, columns <= 12; 1 <= len(words) <= 3 * 10^4; 1 <= len(word) <= 10; letters are lowercase English; the words are distinct.

examples.explanation: "tag" fails because g isn't next to a; each of the others can be traced through neighboring cells.
Diagonal moves don't count, so neither "abc" nor "ad" can be spelled.
"aaa" would need to use one of the two cells twice.
